notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Mark 3 below. Fair warning first: there are gaps. I reached my search limit before finding sources for several verses, and I found almost nothing where Protestant traditions clearly disagree with each other.

**Where the notes are thin**
- **Verses with no notes at all:** 10, 15, 18, 23 (beyond what is grouped with vv. 24–26), 25, 28 (except in the v. 29 discussion), 32 and 33.
- **Most of vv. 1–19 comes from just two sources:** David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary (Pentecostal/Calvary Chapel) and Barton W. Johnson's People's New Testament (1891, Restorationist). I didn't reach Gill, Ellicott (except one note on v. 29), the Pulpit Commentary (except one note on vv. 23 and 27) or Precept Austin for these verses.
- **Wesley's Notes:** I found the chapter listing on StudyLight but couldn't open the Mark 3 notes, so there is nothing Methodist here.
- **Lutheran, Pentecostal-specific and Orthodox commentary on this chapter:** I didn't reach any.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith and hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on this chapter.

## Section 1: The traditional reading

**vv. 1–6: Healing in the synagogue**
- **v. 1:** The synagogue was in Capernaum (People's NT). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
  - Guzik passes on Adam Clarke's point: the man's hand was withered, but he could still walk, and he used his feet to get to worship, which is where Jesus met him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
- **v. 2:** By expecting Jesus to heal, the critics were admitting He had God's power. They knew about Him but didn't know Him (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - People's NT says these were the same fault-finders as in chapter 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **v. 3:** Jesus knew what they were thinking. He chose to make the healing public: on the Sabbath, in the synagogue, in front of everyone (People's NT). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **v. 4:** The question hits back at the critics. They were the ones planning a killing while He was saving a life, so which of them was really breaking the Sabbath? (People's NT). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
  - Guzik: there is never a wrong day to do real good. He says the traditions of the time let you stop a cut from bleeding but not put ointment on it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
- **v. 5:** This is one of the few places Jesus is said to be angry, and His anger is at hard hearts. Guzik thinks Jesus chose this time and place on purpose to force a response. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - Telling the man to stretch out a hand he couldn't move shows, in Guzik's words, that God never commands without enabling. Clarke adds that the cure came while the man was obeying. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - People's NT reads the anger as indignation, and the hardness as seen in their fault-finding and their silence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **v. 6:** Two groups who were normally opponents joined to destroy Jesus. Guzik quotes Wiersbe that the Herodians were a political group backing Herod, not a religious party. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - People's NT suggests the Pharisees probably hoped to get Herod, who ruled Galilee, to have Jesus killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html

**vv. 7–12: The crowds**
- **vv. 7–8:** Idumea is the old Edom, south of the Dead Sea, settled by Esau's descendants. Herod the Great's family came from there on his father's side (People's NT). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
  - Guzik thinks the crowd came more for the miracles than the message, and warns that people drawn by what Jesus can do for them don't last. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
- **v. 9:** The "boat" was a fishing boat. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **vv. 11–12:** Guzik quotes William Lane: the demons shouted Jesus' identity to try to control Him, on the old belief that knowing someone's exact name gives you power over them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - Arend Remmers' introduction to Mark notes that Mark often records Jesus asking for His deeds to be kept quiet, and v. 12 is one example. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/mark.html

**vv. 13–19: The Twelve**
- **v. 13:** Jesus was at a turning point, facing plots and shallow crowds. Guzik notes that Luke 6:12 says He prayed all night, and then chose leaders to train. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
- **v. 14:** The first calling was simply to "be with Him." Being sent out came second, and a preacher is only as useful as his time with Jesus (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - People's NT says they were to stay with Him to be trained to preach Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **v. 16:** Jesus had already given Simon the name Peter (John 1:42). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **v. 17:** People's NT says we aren't told why James and John were called "Sons of Thunder," perhaps for their preaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
  - Guzik links it to their fiery temper (Luke 9:54). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
- **vv. 16–19 (the list):** The group included brothers, fishing partners, and political enemies: Matthew worked with Rome as a tax collector, while Simon the Zealot hated Rome. There are brothers (James and John, Peter and Andrew); business associates (Peter, James, and John were all fishermen); political opponents (Matthew, the Roman-collaborating tax collector, and Simon, the Roman-hating zealot); and one who would betray Jesus (Judas Iscariot). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - Guzik on the names:
    - The KJV/NKJV word "Cananite" (BSB "Zealot") marks Simon as a Zealot and has nothing to do with Canaan.
    - Geldenhuys thinks "Iscariot" means "man from Kerioth," which would make Judas the only Judean among the Twelve.
    - The names seem to be listed in pairs, which fits Jesus sending them out two by two.
    - Jesus knew from the start what Judas would do when He chose him.

    https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/

**vv. 20–35: Family and scribes**
- **v. 20:** The crowds were so eager, and Jesus so ready to help, that there was no time to eat (People's NT). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **v. 21:** "His own people" means His family and close friends. Guzik lists reasons they might have worried: He left a trade, faced death threats, became famous, picked unlikely disciples, and was skipping meals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - Gill reads "beside himself" as meaning His zeal had carried Him too far, not that He was literally mad. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/mark/3-21.html
  - The Bible Hub study notes see a mix of real concern, family embarrassment and spiritual misunderstanding. This same family will later stand with the believers (Acts 1:14), proving God's grace can turn misunderstanding into faith. https://biblehub.com/mark/3-21.htm
- **v. 22:** People's NT says these scribes came from the same Jerusalem bodies that later sent Jesus to His death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
  - Barnes says the charge was that Jesus had made a pact with the prince of the devils. The scribes, who came from Jerusalem to watch his conduct, charged him with having made a compact or agreement with the prince of the devils. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/3-27.htm
- **vv. 23–26:** The Pulpit Commentary says Jesus here plainly affirms that Satan is a person with a real kingdom. Observe here that our Lord distinctly affirms the personality of Satan, and a real kingdom of evil. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/3-27.html
  - Coffman makes a similar point: Satan isn't stupid and wouldn't wreck his own kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/3-27.html
- **v. 27:** Satan is the strong man, and Jesus is stronger, freeing people one at a time (Guzik). "I'm not under Satan. Instead, I am proving that I am stronger than he is." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
  - Coffman thinks this implies Jesus had already bound Satan at the temptation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/3-27.html
  - Ligonier (Reformed) says Jews of the time expected the Messiah to bind the devil, and points to Isaiah 49:24–26. In binding the strong man—Satan—and taking back what this vile enemy has claimed for himself, Jesus proves His messianic vocation https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/binding-strong-man
- **v. 29:** Ellicott says Satan's sin is one whose effects and punishment last forever. He says the Greek reads "guilty of an eternal sin" and that "eternal judgment" is a better rendering than "damnation." https://biblehub.com/mark/3-29.htm
  - Gill calls it a sin that can never be blotted out. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ubv/mark/3-29.html
- **v. 30:** People's NT: it was blasphemy against the Spirit because Jesus did His works by the Spirit's power, and they credited them to an unclean spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
- **v. 31:** Guzik suggests the family may have come to carry out the plan in v. 21 and take Him home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/
- **vv. 34–35:** Jesus says obeying God makes the deepest family bond. https://biblehub.com/mark/3-21.htm

## Section 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

I didn't find clear disagreement within Protestantism on this chapter. Here is the closest I got:

- **v. 29 (the unforgivable sin):** John Piper (Baptist) says the scribes aren't told they have committed it; it is a warning, and they may or may not have. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/beyond-forgiveness-blasphemy-against-the-spirit
  - Piper's key point is that this blasphemy puts a person beyond repentance, and therefore beyond forgiveness. So v. 29 isn't really an exception to v. 28. Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit puts you beyond repentance, and therefore beyond forgiveness. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/beyond-forgiveness-blasphemy-against-the-spirit
  - Piper also uses the verse as clear evidence for eternal punishment. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/beyond-forgiveness-blasphemy-against-the-spirit
  - Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary adds that this sin would mean opposing the Spirit's gifts after Christ ascended. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/3-27.htm
  - StudyLight's v. 27 page groups its commentators as Calvinist, Arminian and Dispensational, but I didn't find a real difference of meaning between them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/3-27.html
- **v. 31 (Jesus' brothers):** A Catholic Answers article reports that John Calvin said Matthew 1:25 doesn't let us conclude anything about what happened after Jesus' birth. That suggests not every Reformer read the "brothers" as Mary's sons. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/answering-objections-to-marys-perpetual-virginity
  - People's NT, by contrast, says the obvious reading is that they were Mary's sons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pnt/mark-3.html
  - Desiring God says the same. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/mary-did-you-know

## Section 3: Other views

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes)**
- **v. 21:** Some early "Western" manuscripts change the text so that it is the scribes, not the family, who call Jesus mad. The NET notes say this change was obviously made to avoid embarrassment, and treat it as not original. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Mar+3%3A20-30&theme=wiki
  - The Greek word for "restrain" is also used for "arrest" elsewhere in Mark. Mark places the scribes' story between two family scenes, likely to show the family misread Jesus too. It is probably Mark's intention in this structure to show that Jesus' family is to be regarded as not altogether unlike the experts in the law [scribes] https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=mar&chapter=3&verse=21
- **vv. 22–27:** Beelzebul is another name for Satan. The two parables show the scribes' charge makes no sense, and Jesus' healings show the war is being won and the kingdom is coming. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Mar+3%3A20-30&theme=wiki
- **v. 29:** The NET notes give three points:
  1. The sin is crediting the Spirit's obvious work to Satan.
  2. It is a settled opposition, not a passing doubt.
  3. Someone worried that they have committed it probably hasn't.

  https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Mar+3%3A20-30&theme=wiki

**Catholic and Orthodox**
- **v. 29:** Bible Hub cites Augustine (Sermon 71) as calling this sin final impenitence, meaning refusing to repent to the end. It says the church fathers agreed the sin can't be forgiven because the heart is hardened, not because God arbitrarily refuses. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_blasphemy_unforgivable_in_Mark_3_29.htm
- **vv. 31–32:** The Catechism says the "brothers" were not Mary's children. It points out that James and Joseph, named as Jesus' brothers, are the sons of "the other Mary." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-case-for-marys-perpetual-virginity
  - Another option, from the early *Protoevangelium of James*, is that they were Joseph's sons, which would explain why they felt free to correct Jesus. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/was-mary-a-perpetual-virgin
  - A third Catholic Answers view, citing Hegesippus and Eusebius, makes them cousins. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/was-mary-a-perpetual-virgin
  - The OCA's question-and-answer page sets out the options (Joseph's sons from a previous marriage, adopted, or cousins) and notes that many Protestants say they were Mary's sons. https://www.oca.org/questions/romancatholicism/the-perpetual-virginity-of-mary
  - Guzik calls perpetual virginity contrary to the plain meaning of the Bible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-3/

**Debated popular teaching**
- **v. 27 ("binding the strong man"):** GotQuestions argues against using this verse as a spiritual-warfare method. Never does Jesus instruct us to "bind the strong man" or tell us how to do it. We do not have warrant to interpret the parable as a spiritual reality over geographical regions. https://www.gotquestions.org/bind-the-strongman.html
